nameStory: The Cookie-cutter Sea Star gets its delightful name from its distinctive pentagonal shape that looks remarkably like a sugar cookie cut with a star-shaped cookie cutter. Unlike the familiar five-armed sea stars we usually picture, this species has such short, stubby arms that it appears almost perfectly star-shaped when viewed from above, just like fresh-baked holiday cookies.
description: The Cookie-cutter Sea Star is a chunky, flattened sea star that looks more like a pentagonal cushion than the typical long-armed starfish. It grows to about 3-4 inches across, with five very short, thick arms that barely extend beyond its rounded central body. The upper surface is covered in small, granular plates that give it a rough, sandy texture, while the underside is pale and soft with tiny tube feet.

idTips.label: Pentagon shape
idTips.description: The body forms an almost perfect five-sided shape with arms so short they're barely noticeable - like a geometric cookie rather than a typical starfish

idTips.label: Granular texture
idTips.description: The upper surface feels like coarse sandpaper, covered in tiny bumps and granules that give it a distinctly rough, gritty feel when touched

idTips.label: Thick profile
idTips.description: The body is surprisingly chunky and cushion-like, much thicker than most flat sea stars - almost puffy in appearance

idTips.label: Brownish coloration
idTips.description: Usually dull brown to grayish-brown on top, sometimes with darker mottling, blending in perfectly with muddy sea floors

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Rarely exceeds 4 inches across, making it one of the smaller sea stars you'll encounter in New England waters

habitat: Cookie-cutter Sea Stars live on soft, muddy or sandy sea floors in deeper coastal waters, typically 30-300 feet deep off the New England coast. They prefer areas with fine sediments where they can partially bury themselves, often found alongside other bottom-dwelling creatures like sea cucumbers and brittle stars. You're most likely to encounter one if you're scuba diving or if one gets brought up in fishing nets or dredging operations.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm, beginning to move more frequently across the sea floor in search of food. This is when they're most likely to be spotted by divers.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're actively feeding and may be found closer to shore in slightly shallower waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to slow down as temperatures drop. May start moving to slightly deeper waters.
seasonality.winter: Least active, often remaining buried or motionless in the sediment. Rarely observed during this season except in deeper, more stable waters.

funFact: Cookie-cutter Sea Stars are living vacuum cleaners of the sea floor - they can actually turn their stomach inside out and extend it outside their body to digest organic matter in the mud, essentially eating the sea floor itself and extracting nutrients from decomposing material.
confusionNotes: Most people confuse this with cushion stars or other short-armed sea stars, but the Cookie-cutter's perfectly pentagonal shape is the giveaway - think 'geometric cookie' rather than 'stubby starfish.' If it looks like it was cut with a cookie cutter, you've found the right species.
contextualKnowledge: This is one of the few sea stars that's truly adapted for a burrowing lifestyle rather than clinging to rocks, which explains why it looks so different from the classic starfish shape most people expect to see.
compareHints: Since this is the only Ctenodiscus species in New England waters, compare it to cushion stars (Asterina species) which are much smaller and more circular, or mud stars which have more pronounced arms. The Cookie-cutter's perfect pentagon shape and granular texture make it unique among New England sea stars - no other local species has quite this geometric, cookie-like appearance.
